title: Chapter 15 — Chowder
paragraphs: It was late in the evening when the little Moss came snugly to anchor, and Queequeg and I went ashore. We couldn't attend to any business that day — nothing but supper and a bed. The landlord of the Spouter-Inn had recommended us to his cousin Hosea Hussey of the Try Pots, who he claimed ran one of the best hotels in all Nantucket and was famous for his chowders. In short, he strongly hinted we couldn't do better than try our luck at the Try Pots. But his directions — keep a yellow warehouse on your starboard until you see a white church to port, then keep that to port until you reach a corner three points to starboard, then ask the first person you meet — confused us badly. Especially since Queequeg insisted the yellow warehouse should be to port, while I was sure Peter Coffin had said starboard. After stumbling around in the dark for a while, occasionally waking a peaceful resident to ask directions, we finally came to something unmistakable.

Two enormous wooden pots, painted black and suspended by handles, swung from the crossbeams of an old topmast planted in front of an old doorway. The opposite ends of the crossbeams had been sawn off, making the topmast look disturbingly like a gallows. Maybe I was oversensitive at the time, but I couldn't help staring at it with a vague dread. My neck felt stiff as I gazed up at the two remaining arms — yes, two of them: one for Queequeg, one for me. Ominous, I thought. A Coffin for an innkeeper at my first whaling port; tombstones staring at me in the whalemen's chapel; and now a gallows! Plus a pair of enormous black pots! Were these throwing out hints about Hell?

I was pulled from these reflections by the sight of a freckled woman with yellow hair and a yellow dress, standing in the porch under a dull red lamp that looked like a bruised eye, having a brisk argument with a man in a purple wool shirt.
'Get along with you,' she said to the man, 'or I'll give you a thrashing!'
'Come on, Queequeg,' I said. 'That's Mrs. Hussey.'

And so it was. Mr. Hosea Hussey was away, but Mrs. Hussey was entirely capable of managing everything. When we told her we wanted supper and a bed, she paused her scolding, led us into a little room, sat us at a table covered with the remains of a recent meal, turned to us and said: 'Clam or cod?'
'What's that about cod, ma'am?' I said politely.
'A clam for supper? A cold clam? Is that what you mean, Mrs. Hussey?' I said. 'That's rather cold and clammy for a winter reception, isn't it?'

But being in a great hurry to resume scolding the man in the purple shirt, who was waiting in the hall, and apparently hearing only the word 'clam,' Mrs. Hussey rushed to an open kitchen door, yelled 'Clam for two!' and disappeared.
'Queequeg,' I said, 'do you think we can make a supper out of one clam?'

But a warm, savory steam from the kitchen belied the cheerless prospect. When the smoking chowder arrived, the mystery was deliciously explained. Oh, friends, listen to me! It was made of small, juicy clams barely bigger than hazelnuts, mixed with crushed ship biscuit and salt pork cut into little flakes, the whole enriched with butter and generously seasoned with pepper and salt. Our appetites sharpened by the frosty voyage, and Queequeg especially delighted to see his favorite seafood, we demolished it at great speed. The chowder was supremely excellent. Then, leaning back and remembering Mrs. Hussey's 'clam or cod' announcement, I decided to try an experiment. I stepped to the kitchen door, pronounced the word 'cod' with great emphasis, and sat back down. In a few moments the savory steam returned, but with a different flavor, and presently a fine cod chowder was placed before us.

We got back to business. Plying our spoons, I thought: I wonder if chowder has any effect on the brain? What's that expression about 'chowder-headed' people? 'But look, Queequeg — isn't that a live eel in your bowl? Where's your harpoon?'

The fishiest of all fishy places was the Try Pots, which fully deserved its name — the pots were always boiling with chowder. Chowder for breakfast, chowder for dinner, chowder for supper, until you started expecting fish bones to come through your clothes. The yard was paved with clam shells. Mrs. Hussey wore a polished necklace of codfish vertebrae, and Hosea Hussey's account books were bound in superior old sharkskin. Even the milk tasted fishy, which I couldn't explain until one morning, strolling along the beach among the fishing boats, I saw Hosea's cow feeding on fish scraps and marching along the sand with each foot stuck in a decapitated cod's head — looking very slovenly, I assure you.

After supper, we received a lamp and directions from Mrs. Hussey to the nearest bed. But as Queequeg was about to go up the stairs ahead of me, she reached out her arm and demanded his harpoon. No harpoons in her rooms. 'Why not?' I said. 'Every true whaleman sleeps with his harpoon.' 'Because it's dangerous,' she said. 'Ever since young Stiggs came back from that unfortunate voyage — gone four and a half years with only three barrels of oil — and was found dead in my first-floor back room with his harpoon in his side, I allow no boarders to take such dangerous weapons to their rooms at night. So, Mr. Queequeg' — she had learned his name — 'I'll just take this iron and keep it for you till morning. But the chowder — clam or cod for breakfast, men?'
'Both,' I said. 'And let's have a couple of smoked herrings for variety.'
